source_document.body:
The European Union's flag (Photo: European Council of Ministers)
WASHINGTON — For the first time, the 27 member states of the European Union (EU) officially have given approval for a collective response — via political, economic or even military means — to threats against any one nation’s satellites and related terrestrial infrastructure, under a recent decision by the group’s ruling Council of Ministers.
The key tenet of the multifaceted Sept. 23 Council Decision 2026/2195 is a green light for joint action, according to several US and European analysts.
“This framework aims to do the same thing as the recent US disclosure of on-orbit space control weapons : deterring space threats,” said Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Aerospace Security Project. “Europe is looking at space threats as a collective threat, not just as a threat to one nation. Accordingly, it’s prepared to respond as Europe rather than just as one country.”
Michael Gleason, a long-time expert on the EU at The Aerospace Corporation’s Center for Space Policy and Strategy, agreed. The upshot of the decision, he said, is that “if a member state says that they want the EU to help them respond, then the EU could make a decision to do so.”
Further, Gleason said the move is one more step in the EU’s long-running, but recently accelerated, effort to create “ strategic autonomy ” in the space arena.
“This is consistent with what the EU’s plans have been, and going forward, we’re going to see a lot more widening and deepening of other space initiatives in the space security and defense arena,” he added.
The decision document outlines measures to both broaden and expand the EU’s Space Threat Response Architecture created in 2021, which empowered the EU to respond to threats against jointly owned/operated satellite systems, such as Europe’s version of GPS Galileo and the Copernicus remote sensing constellation. It also enhances the ability of the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy ― the EU’s top diplomat for security-related issues ― to unilaterally take action if an urgent response is required.
The new Council Decision “expands the scope of the EU’s response space threats to the security of the EU, the security of Member States or both even if they are not directly linked to the EU space assets,” according to an EU fact sheet .
“In short, it strengthens and adapts the existing architecture to the current space threat environment. This includes, for example, cyber-attacks and espionage, but also possible disruptions to supply chains, ground stations or the wider space-based infrastructure,” the fact sheet adds.
The decision can be read as an outgrowth of the EU’s framework space security and defense strategy published in 2023, said Xavier Pasco, senior researcher at France’s Foundation for Strategic Research.
The strategy initiated the creation by the EU headquarters of a common threat picture, called upon member states to strengthen their individual response capabilities, and urged them to at least consider whether joint action might be necessary.
Whereas the 2023 document laid out “more indirect approaches” for threat response, the new Council Decision “focuses more on the role the EU would play in more direct strategies for protection, threat identification, etc,” he told Breaking Defense.
The move could be particularly important for Austria, Cyprus, Ireland and Malta, the four EU members that are not also members of NATO and thus not covered by the alliance’s Article 5 mutual defense pact. And for those members in both groups, this new system also offers a different pathway should NATO not choose to respond for whatever reason .
Of course, as Swope pointed out, the new decision is only an enabling document. It does not add any new military capabilities to EU members arsenals; nor does it guarantee the EU will have the political will to actually go all the way to military action in response to threats or low-level attacks.
“[T]he question is whether Europe’s collective teeth have sufficient bite to deter hostile space activities, particularly ones from Russia. Whether from one country or 27, Russia seems happy to ignore diplomatic naming and shaming,” he said. “Can this unified approach ramp up the consequences enough to produce a different result?”
